question.text: Scenario: Mr. Arvind Sharma, aged 42, is a senior manager at an IT company earning Rs. 18 lakh per annum (gross). His wife Mrs. Priya works part-time earning Rs. 6 lakh per annum. Their combined monthly expenses are Rs. 1,20,000. They have two children aged 14 and 10. Arvind's current investments include: Equity Mutual Funds Rs. 35 lakh, PPF Rs. 12 lakh (current balance), Bank Fixed Deposits Rs. 8 lakh, Employee PF balance Rs. 18 lakh, and a savings bank balance of Rs. 3 lakh. He has an outstanding home loan of Rs. 22 lakh with EMI of Rs. 25,000/month (included in expenses above) and no other loans. His employer contributes Rs. 1,800/month to PF and he contributes the same. He wants to retire at age 58 and needs a retirement corpus of Rs. 3 crore. He also needs Rs. 30 lakh for his elder child's education in 4 years and Rs. 25 lakh for the younger child in 8 years. Assume equity returns at 12% CAGR and debt returns at 7% CAGR. Inflation is 6% p.a. Question 2 of 5: What is the Sharma family's investment assets net of the home loan (i.e., total investments minus the outstanding home loan, excluding the self-occupied home value)?

explanation.text: The Logic: Total investment assets = 35 + 12 + 8 + 18 + 3 = Rs. 76 lakh. Subtracting the outstanding home loan of Rs. 22 lakh gives Rs. 54 lakh as investment assets net of the home loan. The Trap: Rs. 76 lakh is the total of investment assets only and does not net off the home loan that is being deducted. Note: True net worth would require adding the market value of the self-occupied home to the asset side; here the home value is not given, so the figure is intentionally framed as investment assets net of the home-loan liability rather than as a full net-worth calculation.
